Designing browser games for more ways to play

A source-based overview of selected NoCharge input and feedback choices, with clear limits: individual controls vary, and this is not an accessibility certification.

By NoCharge·Reviewed by NoCharge·Published August 19, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read
Check the current platform.

Use the public pages behind this explanation.

Open the ArcadeReview PrivacyKeyboard-only play notes

Bottom line: Input support is game-specific. The current Arcade pages describe each title’s actual controls; this article is a design and testing note, not a claim that every game works with every device or assistive technology.

Start with the game’s own controls

Some current games expose labeled board cells or buttons that can be activated with Enter or Space; others use a different interaction pattern. A page may also offer row-and-column selectors as an alternate to choosing a small board cell. Read the controls on the specific Arcade page rather than assuming a single input method is available everywhere.

When reviewing a game, check whether the active turn, selection, result, and rejected moves are communicated in text as well as through color or movement. Optional sound should not be treated as the only source of game state. Reduced-motion settings, browser zoom, focus order, and target size are separate considerations, not proof of universal compatibility.

What automated checks can and cannot show

Automated tests can exercise the routes and controls they explicitly visit and check selected properties such as labels, focus behavior, layout overflow, and contrast. They cannot replace manual use with screen readers, physical keyboards, touch devices, magnification, high contrast, or different browsers. Passing a selected test suite is evidence about those checks only.

The companion keyboard-only browser games article discusses the limits of keyboard claims. NoCharge does not claim a completed universal-device audit or accessibility certification here.
